studies.title: We Narrate To You
studies.meaning: Three letters, then a claim about the book, then a statement of method. We recite to you part of the report of Moses and Pharaoh, in truth, for people who believe. Two things in that sentence repay attention. It says part, not all, so the narrative that follows is selected rather than complete. And it names its audience before the story starts, which makes the telling conditional on someone willing to take it as more than history.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, late in the period before the emigration. Commentators report no specific occasion for these ayat. What matters for the surah's argument is who was listening: a small community under pressure in a city they did not control, about to be told at length how a comparable situation once developed. The surah never draws the parallel out loud. It sets the account down and leaves it there.

keyTerms.note: The Arabic form is open between clear in itself and making other things clear, and the commentators note both readings. Either way the claim concerns the book's function rather than its style.
Not any news, but news of consequence arriving from elsewhere. The word implies the account was carried to the hearer rather than worked out by him or recalled from his own memory.
The phrase attaches to the manner of the telling. It claims accuracy, and commentators also read it as telling for a purpose, since the same word covers what is right as well as what is real.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories about earlier peoples were currency in Mecca. Traders brought them back from Syria and Yemen, and rival storytellers competed with tales of Persian kings for the same audiences the recitation was addressing. Claiming to give a true report of Moses in that market was not a neutral act. It was entering a contest the listeners already knew how to judge.
studies.didYouKnow: The three letters opening this surah begin only one other surah in the Quran, the one immediately before it. Those two sit side by side and both retell the Moses narrative at length, from different angles. The phrase about the clear book that follows the letters appears at the head of five surahs in all, and nowhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Narrative is presented as revelation rather than as illustration. The account is recited, using the same verb employed for reciting the signs, which places the story on the same footing as any other part of the message. And the closing qualification concedes something openly: the account will do its work for people who believe, and will function as one more old tale for everybody else.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same three letters and begins its own version of the Moses account.
Introduces the same narrative with a question, asking whether the report has reached you.
Calls its narrative the best of accounts, and says the hearer was unaware of it.

studies.applyIt: Read a story you know well from scripture as though you had never heard it. Take one paragraph and ask what you would notice if it arrived today with no ending attached. This ayah says the account is given for people who believe, which is not a boast. It describes a way of listening you can choose before you start.

studies.title: Divided Into Factions
studies.meaning: Pharaoh's rule is described in four verbs and the order is deliberate. He raised himself above the land, then split its people into factions, then singled out one faction to weaken, then killed their sons and kept their daughters alive. The division comes before the persecution. Commentators note that this is stated as a method rather than as a list of crimes, and the closing verdict calls him a corrupter rather than a tyrant.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah opens its narrative not with Moses but with the system he was born into, which is unusual. No occasion of revelation is reported. The Meccan audience included a small group being squeezed by a leadership that controlled the city's trade, its shrine and its alliances, and a description of a divided population under one exalted figure needed no explaining.

keyTerms.note: A verb of elevation used of a person raising himself over others. It is the first thing said about him, so everything after it is presented as following from that self elevation.

Groups formed by attachment to a leader or a cause. The word appears four times in the Quran and the others describe communities that fractured, so dividing a population is being named here as an act.
From the root for spoiling something sound. The verdict is not that he was cruel but that he ruined a working arrangement, which is a claim about the whole order he was running.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian politics ran on alliances between clans, and the reliable way to control a confederation was to keep its parts from combining. A leader who could set two clans against each other did not need an army. The audience for this ayah understood the mechanism from the inside, since their own city's hierarchy was maintained by exactly that kind of managed division.
studies.didYouKnow: The killing of the sons is described in several places across the Quran, and this is the only one where it is preceded by the splitting of the population into factions. Everywhere else the persecution is reported on its own terms. This surah alone supplies the political method that made it workable, and it puts that first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Oppression is analysed rather than merely condemned. The passage identifies self-exaltation as the root and division as the instrument, which locates the wrong inside a structure rather than only in a personality. And the summary verdict uses the language of corruption, so the charge is not that he broke a rule but that he damaged something, which is how this Book generally assesses power.

crossReferences.why: Recalls the same persecution to the Children of Israel as the trial they were delivered from.
Shows the same order given again later, after Moses arrives with the message.
Uses the same word for factions, as one of the calamities a community can be given.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the moment a group you are in gets sorted into camps, and notice who benefits from the sorting. It is rarely the people in either camp. You do not have to name it out loud. Just be able to say to yourself who gains when a room divides, and decline to help it along.

studies.title: We Intended To Favour Them
studies.meaning: The counter-statement is placed immediately after the description of the system, and it is in the present tense: We intend. The ones being made weak are the ones to be favoured, made leaders, made inheritors, established in the land. And Pharaoh and his minister are to be shown, from among those same people, the very thing they feared. Commentators note that the whole reversal is announced before the story begins, so nothing that follows is suspense. It is an outcome already stated, arriving.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the timing matters. The community hearing this had no land, no power and no near prospect of either, and would not emigrate for some time yet. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. What they offered was a description of a comparable situation whose ending was already known, given to people whose own ending was not.

keyTerms.note: A verb for conferring something unearned. Its noun also covers a favour held over someone's head, so the Quran is careful about who may use it, and here the subject is God alone.
A passive form of a verb meaning to treat someone as weak. It names weakness as something done to them rather than as a quality they had, which the previous ayah described in detail.
Those who receive what someone else leaves behind. Using the word here means the land does not change hands by conquest in this account; it passes to them the way an estate passes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance was the most litigated matter in Arabian life. Who received a man's camels, his wells and his debts was decided by lineage and argued over for generations, and the vocabulary was familiar to everyone. Promising a persecuted group they would be the inheritors used the one legal category that transferred property without a fight, and every listener knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The name of Pharaoh's minister appears six times in the Quran, and all six belong to this narrative, two of them in these opening ayat alone. He is named beside Pharaoh as though the pairing were standard, yet he is given no title, no lineage and no words of his own until much later in this same surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The announcement comes before the events and in a tense that keeps it open, which changes what the story is for. It is not evidence that God rescues, offered after the fact, but a stated intention the reader then watches being carried out through a chain of ordinary decisions. What follows is a mother's fear, a sister's errand and a household's whim, and none of them look like the fulfilment of anything.

crossReferences.why: Records the same inheritance completed, the weakened people given the land's east and west.
States the general principle, that the earth is inherited by God's righteous servants.
Gives the final home to those who seek neither height nor corruption in the land.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are waiting on that shows no visible movement. Now notice that in this passage the outcome is announced first, and the story is then made entirely of small ordinary events that do not look like progress. Pick one small ordinary thing in your own situation this week and do it well, without checking whether it counts.

studies.title: Cast Him Into The River
studies.meaning: An instruction is given to a woman who is not a prophet, and it is close to unbearable. Nurse him, and when you fear for him, put him in the water. Then two prohibitions and two promises: do not fear, do not grieve, We will return him to you, and We will make him one of the messengers. The next line reports the pickup in words that read like an accident. The household that took him in did not know what it was carrying home.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Commentators discuss the verb used for the communication to Moses' mother and generally take it as inspiration placed in the heart rather than prophethood, since the Quran uses the same verb for what is conveyed to a bee and to the disciples. No occasion of revelation is reported. The narrative belongs to the surah's opening movement, which turns entirely on a decision made under threat.

keyTerms.note: The verb usually rendered as revelation, though this Book also uses it of what is placed in a bee and in the earth. Commentators here read a communication to the heart rather than prophethood.
A word for a large body of water, used in the Quran almost only within this narrative. It leaves open whether a river or a sea is meant, and the classical accounts differ on the point.
A verb for retrieving something found by chance, occurring once in the Quran. The same root gives the ordinary word for a foundling, so the wording preserves the household's own view of the event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A newborn was not a private matter. Wet nurses were hired, births were announced, and a household's infants were known to its neighbours. Concealing a baby for any length of time meant concealing sound, and anyone who has kept a secret in a crowded house knows the cost of it. The instruction here is addressed to a woman who had already been managing that for months.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for picking him up occurs once in the Quran, and its root gives the ordinary Arabic word for a foundling, a child retrieved without anyone knowing whose it is. The clause that follows says he was picked up in order to become their enemy and their sorrow, which states as purpose what the finders experienced as chance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a promise and an unbearable instruction in the same sentence, in that order, and softens neither. The two prohibitions come after the command rather than before it, which suggests fear and grief were expected and were being addressed rather than forbidden. And the outcome is tied to the finders' action by a clause of purpose, so what looked to them like luck is described as an errand.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same episode in the parallel account, including the sister and the return.
Uses the same verb of inspiration for what is conveyed to the bee.
Names the woman of Pharaoh's household as an example, for the prayer she made.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you had to let something out of your hands: a child at a gate, a decision passed to someone else, an application sent. Recall the physical moment of release. The instruction here arrives with two prohibitions attached, which means the fear and the grief were expected. You are not doing it wrong when they turn up.

studies.title: A Delight To The Eye
studies.meaning: One sentence from Pharaoh's wife changes the outcome. She calls the child a coolness of the eye for the two of them, forbids the killing, and gives two reasons calculated to appeal to her husband: he may be useful, or we might take him as a son. Then the narrator adds four words. They did not perceive. Commentators note that her stated argument is entirely practical, while the phrase she opens with is the language of love.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Quran gives this woman no name here and returns to her once, near the end of the Book, as an example held up for everyone. Commentators say little beyond what the text supplies. No occasion of revelation is reported. What the passage records is a decision taken inside the household that had ordered the killing, by someone with standing enough to be heard.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for deep contentment, drawn from tears of joy running cool rather than hot. This exact phrase occurs once in the Quran, and a related plural appears twice in prayers about family.
A particle of hope and possibility. She offers two speculative reasons rather than one certainty, which is how a person argues when the real reason is not the one being placed on the table.
A verb of adopting or taking something for a purpose. It appears in this Book for taking gods, taking friends and taking a child, and it always implies a deliberate choosing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Taking a foundling into a household was ordinary and legally consequential in Arabia. A child raised in a family shared its protection and its enemies, and the arrangement was announced rather than hidden. Her second suggestion was therefore not sentimental. It named a recognised standing that would place the boy inside the very house which had ordered his death.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase she uses occurs in exactly this form only here in the Quran. Four ayat later the same image returns in a different form, when the child is given back to his mother so that her eye may be cooled. The wording ties the two women together, and it is the only thing in the account that does.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reversal announced at the surah's opening is carried forward by a woman's affection for an infant she had no reason to spare. Nothing miraculous occurs. The passage insists twice within a few lines on the absence of foresight, which makes its point about how such outcomes are actually produced: not by anyone in the story understanding what they are doing, but by ordinary motives arriving at the right moment.

crossReferences.why: Returns to this woman near the end of the Quran, quoting her prayer as an example.
Repeats her image of the cooled eye, transferred to the mother who had lost him.
Shows another household taking in a boy for his usefulness, in similar words of adoption.

studies.applyIt: Notice the reason you give out loud for a kindness you are about to do, and how often it is a practical one when the real reason is affection. There is nothing wrong with that translation; it is how most kindness gets past a room. But be honest with yourself about which of the two actually moved you.

studies.title: Her Heart Went Empty
studies.meaning: One word describes what happened to the mother: her heart became empty. Commentators offer several readings, that it emptied of everything except him, or of patience, or of the promise she had been given, and they set the range down without choosing. She was close to saying it aloud, and the ayah states plainly that she was steadied so she would remain among the believers. Then the practical response: she sends her daughter after him, and the girl watches from a distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The account is unusual in giving this much interior detail about a woman who is never named, and the parallel version in surah 20 compresses the same events into a few lines. No occasion of revelation is reported. Commentators treat the sequence as an instance of what the surah has already announced, an outcome arriving through people who do not know they are producing it.

keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran. The root covers being emptied out and being free of occupation, which is why the classical readings differ over what exactly her heart was emptied of.
A verb for tying something so that it holds. It appears twice in the Quran with the heart as its object, and the other place describes the young men who took refuge in the cave.
An imperative from the root that gives this surah its name. It means tracing something by following its trail, so the sister is told to track him rather than simply to look.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A girl following something along a riverbank would have drawn no attention. Children ran errands, carried water and moved between households all day, and their invisibility was practical rather than accidental. The narrative uses that: the one person in the family who could go anywhere without being questioned is the one who is sent, and she keeps her distance and says nothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for steadying her heart appears twice in the Quran with the heart as its object. The other place describes the youths who hid in the cave, in an entirely different surah and setting. Both times it is applied to people holding a secret under pressure, and both times God is the one said to do the steadying.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not treat her near collapse as a failure. It reports that she was about to give him away and that she was held, and it supplies a reason: so that she would remain among the believers. Faith appears here as something maintained from outside at the exact point where a person's own capacity runs out, which is a considerable claim to make inside a narrative.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about hearts being steadied, of young men standing before a ruler.
Gives the sister's part in the parallel account, with the return to the mother.
Uses the same verb for steadying hearts, of a community about to face a battle.

studies.applyIt: Recall a time you nearly said the thing that would have ruined it, and did not. You probably credited yourself with self-control. Try reading it once the way this ayah reads it: as being held rather than as holding on. It changes what you do with the memory, and it changes what you expect of yourself next time.

studies.title: A Household That Will Nurse Him
studies.meaning: The refusal comes first: he would take no wet nurse at all, and the ayah says this had been arranged beforehand. Then the sister steps forward with a sentence built to give nothing away. Shall I point you to a household who will look after him for you, and who will be sincere toward him. Commentators note the wording. She offers a solution to a practical problem, she says for you, and she vouches for the family's goodwill without saying how she knows it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The wet nurse arrangement was a normal part of ancient household life, so the premise would have been immediately clear to the first hearers. No occasion of revelation is reported. The parallel account in surah 20 gives the same sequence in a single line, which is one of several places where this surah slows a familiar narrative down to show the mechanics.

keyTerms.note: The verb of prohibiting, used here of an infant refusing the breast. Commentators read it as an arranged aversion rather than as a rule, since a baby is not addressed by rules.
Occurs once in the Quran. It is a plural covering both the women and the act of suckling, so the refusal described is total: not one nurse but every arrangement that was offered.
From a root meaning pure and unmixed, used of advice given without self interest. She is guaranteeing the household's motive, which is the one thing she had no way to prove.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hiring a wet nurse was routine and often took a child out of the city for years; the Prophet himself was nursed among a desert clan as an infant. Families kept track of the women available, and a healthy baby refusing every one of them would have been an urgent domestic crisis rather than a curiosity. The sister arrives with an answer to a problem the household already had.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the wet nurses occurs once in the Quran. The sentence the sister speaks is built entirely out of the household's own interest: she offers a family who will look after him for you, and vouches for their sincerity toward him. She never says that she knows them, and nobody in the scene thinks to ask.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The arrangement runs entirely through ordinary means. An infant's refusal, a household's inconvenience, a girl's well judged offer. Nothing is suspended and nobody is compelled, and yet the ayah says openly that the refusal had been set up in advance. That combination is the surah's method: an announced outcome delivered through decisions each of which could be explained without reference to God at all.

crossReferences.why: Compresses this whole exchange into a single line in the parallel account.
Holds the promise this scene begins to deliver, that he would be returned to her.
Shows another child placed in a household, with the outcome stated before the story turns.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you ask for something you badly want. Most people either overexplain or lead with their own need. The sister does neither: she names the other person's problem, offers a solution, and stops talking. Try that shape once this week on a small request, and watch how differently it lands in the room.

studies.title: Returned So Her Eye Would Cool
studies.meaning: The promise is kept, and the ayah gives three reasons for it in order: so that her eye would be cooled, so that she would not grieve, and so that she would know God's promise is true. The third is the one the passage cares about, and it comes last. Then years pass in half a line. He reaches full strength and settles, and is given judgement and knowledge, with a closing comment that this is how those who do well are answered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The compression is striking: an infancy, a childhood and a young adulthood inside a single ayah, in a surah that spent five ayat on a basket. No occasion of revelation is reported. The narrative is selecting, exactly as the third ayah of the surah said it would, and what it selects are the moments where somebody learns something.

keyTerms.note: From the idiom about tears of joy running cool. The same phrase appears in the parallel account in surah 20, and it takes up the words of the woman who saved him four ayat earlier.
A plural form with no singular in ordinary use, describing the years when a person's powers are complete. The Quran applies it to Joseph and to Moses at the same turning point in each life.
The capacity to decide rightly, named separately here from knowledge. Commentators note that the pairing describes a formation over years rather than a single moment of appointment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nursing a foster child for pay was a recognised trade and the arrangement was public. A woman nursing her own son under contract to the household that had taken him would have been an entirely ordinary sight, invisible to anyone who did not know. That ordinariness is the point of the scene, and the ayah passes over it in a clause and moves to what he became.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about her eye being cooled appears twice in the Quran, here and in the parallel telling in surah 20. It also answers the phrase used four ayat earlier by the woman in Pharaoh's household, who called the infant a coolness of the eye for herself and her husband. The same image lands on both women.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reunion is granted for a reason the ayah states itself, and the reason is knowledge rather than comfort. She is given her son back so that she will know the promise was true, which makes the episode instruction as much as relief. And the closing clause, that most of them do not know, keeps the lesson particular. What she learned was available only to someone who had first been asked to give something up.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same return in the parallel account, with the identical phrase about her eye.
Uses the same wording for Joseph reaching full strength and being given judgement and knowledge.
States the promise this ayah reports as kept, given at the moment of greatest risk.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you gave up and later received back in an unexpected form. Not everything comes back, and the ayah is not promising that it does. But where it has happened to you, notice what you actually learned from it, and whether you have ever put that into words. Do that today, in one sentence.

studies.title: A Blow He Did Not Mean
studies.meaning: He enters the city at an hour when nobody is paying attention, finds two men fighting, and one of them, from his own people, calls him in. He strikes the other and the man dies. The Arabic verb describes a punch, not a weapon, and his own reaction is immediate: this is from the work of the enemy who misleads. Commentators are careful here, reading the death as an outcome he did not aim at, and noting that his verdict on it arrives before anyone else's.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The episode is told in more detail here than anywhere else in the Quran, and the surah has been building toward it since it described the divided population in its fourth ayah. No occasion of revelation is reported. The word used for the man's own group is the same word used earlier for the factions Pharaoh created, which ties the street fight to the policy.

keyTerms.note: The state of attention having drifted elsewhere. The phrase describing the city occurs once in the Quran, and it places the whole episode in a moment when nobody happened to be looking.
Occurs once in the Quran. Lexicographers gloss it as a blow with the closed hand or the elbow, so the word itself rules out a weapon and makes the death an outcome rather than an aim.
From the same root used earlier in this surah for the factions the population had been divided into. The street quarrel is described in the exact vocabulary of the policy that produced it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A death by a blow was the hardest kind of case in a society without police. There was no forum for settling intent; there was a body, a claimant, and a family owed an answer. Leaving town was the standard response, and it is what happens in the ayat that follow. Everyone hearing this understood the position he was in by the end of the sentence.
studies.didYouKnow: Two expressions in this ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the phrase for the city at an unwatched hour, and the verb for the blow itself. The word for the man's own party, by contrast, is the same one used in the surah's fourth ayah for the factions the population had been split into.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The narrative gives a future prophet an act he immediately assigns to the enemy of humanity, and does not soften it. What follows in the next ayah is not an excuse but a request. The passage is unusual in showing how a wrong actually gets produced: a real grievance, a genuine appeal for help, a moment of anger, and a result nobody intended and nobody can undo.

crossReferences.why: Has Pharaoh raise this same act against him years later, along with Moses' reply.
Refers to the same killing in the parallel account, in a single compressed clause.
Shows Moses citing this death as the reason he fears going back to Egypt.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you stepped into someone else's fight because they asked you to. It is not a bad instinct. But notice how fast the appeal for help removed your own judgement from the situation. Next time somebody pulls you in, take the single second Moses did not take, and ask what you are actually about to do.

studies.title: Never A Support For Wrongdoers
studies.meaning: Two sentences, both beginning the same way. He says he has wronged himself and asks to be forgiven, and the answer arrives inside the same ayah, with no interval and no condition attached. Then a second prayer that is not about the past at all: given what You have favoured me with, I will never be a backer of the guilty. Commentators note the shape. The request concerns what he did; the promise concerns a role he will not take again.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is addressing people who had to decide, repeatedly, whose side to stand on in a city where the powerful were watching closely. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The second sentence, a refusal to be anybody's backing, would have carried a specific weight for a small group being asked, quietly and often, to stay useful to the leadership.

keyTerms.note: The standard formula for admitting a fault in this Book, completed by the word for oneself. The wrong is described as landing on the wrongdoer first, which is a claim about damage rather than a way of minimising it.
The reply comes in the narrative voice and in the past tense, inside the same sentence as the request. Nothing is placed between the asking and the answer, and no condition is attached to it.
From the word for the back. It means the one standing behind another and lending strength. The word occurs four times in the Quran, and twice within this surah alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Backing was the currency of Arabian politics. A man's safety depended on who stood behind him, and withholding or switching that support was the most consequential thing an individual could do. To promise never again to be anyone's backing was not a private resolution. It named a public position, and everyone listening knew what refusing that role would cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Moses uses for a backer occurs four times in the Quran and twice in this surah. The other use here comes near the very end, where the Prophet is told not to be a backer of those who reject. The surah opens its Moses narrative and closes its own argument with the same word, in the same refusal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is granted in the same breath as it is requested, and the narrative does not pause to weigh the asking. What follows is the more interesting part. He does not promise to be better in general; he identifies the specific position that produced the act, standing behind someone because they were his, and closes it off. Repentance appears here as a change of allegiance rather than a change of feeling.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical words of self-wronging at the moment another figure submits.
Repeats the same word for a backer at the close of this surah's argument.
Describes standing up for justice even against yourself and your own near relatives.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you back automatically: a family, a team, a side in an argument you stopped examining years ago. You do not have to leave it. Just find one instance where being their support would mean helping something you know is wrong, and decide in advance, today, what you will do when it comes.

studies.title: Fearful And Watching
studies.meaning: He spends the next morning moving through the city afraid, scanning for what is coming. Then the same man is shouting for him again, in another fight. Moses' response this time is not a blow but a sentence: you are plainly a man who has lost his way. Commentators note that everything has changed in a single day. Nothing about the grievance is different, but the person being called on now knows exactly what his help costs.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah slows to a day by day pace here, having covered whole years in a clause a few ayat earlier. No occasion of revelation is reported. The audience were people who had begun to be watched in their own city, and the phrase describing Moses in the streets, afraid and looking about him, would not have been an unfamiliar sensation to them.

keyTerms.note: A verb for scanning for what is about to arrive. Paired with the word for fearful, it makes a two-word phrase that occurs twice in the Quran, both times in this surah about this man.

keyTerms.gloss: crying out to him for help
keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran. It is a form built from shouting, so this is not a request but a yell across a street, which is why a crowd would already be turning to look.
From the root for losing the way rather than the root for wickedness. Moses is naming the man's judgement rather than his character, which leaves room for him to be right about the grievance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man wanted for a death lived in a particular kind of alertness. There were no walls to hide behind in a working city and no anonymity in a quarter where everybody knew every face. He would have measured each street by its exits. The Arabic phrase for what Moses was doing describes exactly how that looks from outside: walking normally, and looking.
studies.didYouKnow: The two-word phrase describing Moses as fearful and watching occurs twice in the Quran, both in this surah, at ayat 18 and 21, and nowhere else in the Book. The first has him inside the city and the second has him leaving it, so one repeated phrase brackets the whole day between the killing and the flight.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a future prophet be visibly wrong twice in two days: once in the blow, and now in the tone of a rebuke delivered to a man who is being beaten. Neither is excused and neither is treated as disqualifying. What the surah builds is a portrait of someone formed by consequences, which is a different account of prophethood from one that begins with a finished man.

crossReferences.why: Gives the previous day's fight, the appeal for help, and the death it ended in.
Repeats the same phrase about being fearful and watching as he leaves the city.
Records Moses admitting later that he did it while he was among those who stray.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you speak to someone the second time they ask you for the same help. The first time is generous; the second usually comes out sharp, and the sharpness is really about you. You are allowed to say no. Try separating the refusal from the verdict on them, and see whether you can give one without the other.

studies.title: As You Killed Yesterday
studies.meaning: As Moses moves to seize the other man, someone speaks, and one sentence undoes everything. Do you mean to kill me the way you killed a man yesterday? Then the accusation: you only want to be a strongman here, and not one who sets things right. Commentators note an ambiguity the Arabic leaves open about who is speaking, and record both readings. Either way the secret is now out loud in a street with witnesses.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The scene turns on a sentence said in public rather than on any investigation, which fits a city where reputation moved faster than authority did. No occasion of revelation is reported. The surah's audience knew how quickly a remark could reach the people who mattered, and several of them had watched their own conversations arrive at the wrong ears within a day.

keyTerms.note: A verb for laying hold of someone with force. It is stronger than the word used for the blow of the day before, which suggests the second encounter was escalating rather than simply repeating.
The word occurs three times in the Quran. In the other two it is denied of a prophet, said of John and by Jesus of himself. Only here is it thrown at someone as a charge.
From the root for repairing what is damaged, the exact opposite of the word used of Pharaoh in this surah's fourth ayah. The accusation places Moses on the wrong side of that pair.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a society without records, an accusation made in front of witnesses was the nearest thing to evidence. Once several people had heard it, it existed, and it could be repeated to a court or a patron without anyone needing to have seen the act itself. That is why the next ayah has a man running across the city rather than a summons arriving at a door.
studies.didYouKnow: The word thrown at Moses here for an overbearing strongman appears three times in the Quran. The other two both deny it of a prophet: John is described as not being such a man toward his parents, and Jesus says the same of himself. This is the only place where it is an accusation rather than a denial.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A true fact is used as a weapon, and the passage records it without correcting the fact. He had killed a man the day before. The wrong lies in what the sentence is being used to do, which is to stop an intervention and to reframe a person entirely by his worst hour. The Quran lets that stand as a description of how reputation works, and moves the story on.

crossReferences.why: Says of John that he was not an overbearing man, using the word thrown at Moses here.
Has Jesus deny the same quality of himself, in almost identical phrasing.
Gives the killing that this sentence makes public for the first time.

studies.applyIt: Think of one true thing about someone that you keep available in case you ever need it. Everybody has at least one. Notice that its truth is not the issue; the issue is what you are holding it for. Decide today whether to keep holding it, and be honest about what you would be using it to win.

studies.title: A Man Came Running
studies.meaning: Someone crosses the whole city on foot to deliver a warning. He is not named, nothing is said about which group he belongs to, and he never appears again. His message has three parts: the council is conferring about killing you, so get out, and I am among those who wish you well. Commentators note that the same phrase, a man from the farthest part of the city running, occurs once more in the Quran in another scene of urgent warning.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is describing a state of affairs in which decisions about a person's life are taken in a room he is not in, and reach him only if somebody chooses to carry them. No occasion of revelation is reported. That situation was familiar to the first audience, whose safety in Mecca rested on individual protectors rather than on any rule.

keyTerms.note: The far edge of something. The detail is doing work here: the warning comes from a man who had to cross an entire city, so his arrival cost him time and exposure he did not have to spend.
A reciprocal verb from the root of command, occurring once in the Quran. It describes a group issuing instructions to one another, so the decision is collective and already in motion.
The same word Moses' sister used of the household she was recommending. Twice in this surah a stranger's goodwill is asserted rather than demonstrated, and twice it turns out to be genuine.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News moved by foot and by mouth. A man who wanted to warn someone had to go himself, and going meant being seen leaving one quarter and arriving in another. Anyone who noticed could later say where he had been and when. The ayah gives the distance travelled precisely because that distance is what the warning cost the man who brought it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing a man coming from the farthest part of the city, running, occurs twice in the Quran. The other is in surah 36, where a man crosses a town to urge his people to follow the messengers who had reached them. Both men are anonymous, both arrive at a run, and both appear once and are never mentioned again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The rescue at this point runs through a stranger with no stake in the outcome. He is not described as believing anything, and he receives no reward inside the narrative. What the passage records is that the deliverance announced in the surah's opening ayat proceeds through people behaving decently at personal cost, which is a claim about how such things usually arrive.

crossReferences.why: Holds the only other man who comes running from the far end of a city.
Shows a man inside Pharaoh's court who conceals his faith and speaks up for Moses.
Records what Moses does with the warning: he leaves, and prays twice along the way.

studies.applyIt: Someone you know is walking into something and has no idea. You have probably decided it is not your place to say so. Ask what it would actually cost you to say it plainly, once, and then leave it with them. The man in this ayah does not argue or persuade. He delivers the information and names his motive.

studies.title: Perhaps My Lord Will Guide Me
studies.meaning: He leaves the city in the state he woke in, afraid and watching, and prays to be delivered from wrongdoing people. Then, turning toward Madyan, a second prayer: perhaps my Lord will guide me to the even road. Commentators note how different the two are. The first asks to be pulled out of something. The second, said once he is already out, asks only for direction, and it is framed with a particle of hope rather than of request.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Madyan lay north of Egypt along the caravan country, several days of open ground for a man travelling alone and on foot. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The surah's own audience would themselves leave a city under threat within a few years, though nothing in the wording points at that, and the commentators do not press the comparison.

keyTerms.note: A verb for extracting someone from danger. It is the standard prayer of prophets in tight places in this Book, and it asks for removal rather than for victory or for the danger to be ended.
A particle of hope rather than of demand. Placing it before the second prayer keeps that prayer from becoming a claim on God, which is the whole difference between the two sentences.
Literally the levelness of the way. The image is of a road without dips or obstacles, which is exactly what a man crossing unfamiliar country on foot would most want to know about.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving a settlement alone was dangerous in a way that is hard to reconstruct now. Without a guide, a companion or tribal protection, a traveller had no claim on anyone he met and no recourse if he were robbed. Water sources were known to locals and invisible to strangers. Praying for a level road was not a figure of speech for a man in that position.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the even road occurs six times in the Quran. In five of them somebody has strayed from it or led others away from it. This is the only place where a person asks to be brought to it, and it is spoken by a man walking out of one country toward another with no idea where he is going.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two prayers in successive ayat show a change of register that the passage does not comment on. Rescue is asked for in the imperative, while direction is asked for in the language of hope. The second is the harder prayer, because it concedes that being out of danger is not the same as knowing where to go, and it asks for something that will only be recognisable afterwards.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word of deliverance in Noah's prayer, when his own people had turned on him.
Puts the same verb of deliverance in the mouth of the woman who saved Moses as an infant.
Shows what the second prayer actually leads to, which is a well and two strangers.

studies.applyIt: When something you were dreading is finally over, notice that the relief lasts about a day and then a different question arrives: what now. Most people have no prayer for that second moment. Borrow this one. Ask, in whatever words you use, to be shown the level road, and be willing not to recognise it immediately.

studies.title: Two Women Holding Back
studies.meaning: He reaches the water and finds a crowd watering their animals, and off to one side two women keeping their flock away from it. His question is four words in Arabic: what is your situation. Their answer is two sentences that explain everything and complain about none of it. We do not water until the herdsmen have taken theirs off, and our father is a very old man. Commentators note that neither sentence asks him for anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Madyan was a herding and trading region on the routes north, and a well there would have been a shared resource with an informal order of precedence. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The scene is one of very few places in the Quran that describes an everyday economic arrangement in enough detail to see who it disadvantaged.

keyTerms.note: A dual verb occurring once in the Quran, used of driving animals away from something. They are not waiting passively; they are actively keeping their flock off the water while the crowd finishes.
A word for a matter of consequence. The question is neither idle nor intrusive; it asks what the case is, which is how a person addresses strangers whose position he can see is wrong.
Occurs once in the Quran, from the root for shepherding and for looking after something. The same root gives the words used elsewhere for the care a leader owes to those under him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access to water was settled by strength as much as by right. A well served everyone in theory, and in practice the largest flocks and the strongest men went first. Two women with a small flock and no man standing with them would wait until last on any ordinary day, and most people at the well would consider that arrangement normal rather than cruel.
studies.didYouKnow: The dual verb describing the two women holding back their flock occurs once in the Quran, and so does the word used here for the herdsmen. The whole exchange is four short lines of dialogue. Neither woman asks for anything, and the request Moses acts on is one he assembles himself out of two plain statements of fact.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A man on the run, exhausted, with no standing anywhere, notices a small unfairness at a well and puts it right before doing anything at all about his own situation. The passage does not praise him for it in so many words. It simply reports the sequence, and everything he receives afterwards arrives through that action, which is the surah's quiet argument about how provision comes.

crossReferences.why: Gives what he does next, watering for them and then withdrawing to pray alone.
Shows one of the two reporting back what she concluded from watching him work.
Describes the weak who have nobody to stand for them, in the same register.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the queue you always end up at the front of without thinking about it: at work, in a family, in a shop. Somebody is at the back of it for structural reasons rather than by choice. You do not need a campaign about it. Notice one such person this week and move them up one place.

studies.title: I Am In Need
studies.meaning: He waters their flock, withdraws to the shade, and prays a sentence with an unusual shape. My Lord, I am poor toward whatever good You send down to me. He names nothing, and commentators observe how much is left out: no request for food, shelter, safety or a way home. The Arabic makes him poor in relation to what is sent rather than poor in general, so the sentence is about dependence rather than about lack.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Moses has walked out of Egypt with nothing, crossed open country, arrived where he knows no one, and done a stranger's work before resting. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. It sits at the lowest point of the surah's narrative, and it is the last thing he says before anything at all begins to go right for him.

keyTerms.note: The definite form, so it is the shade, a known spot at that well. The detail places him physically: out of the sun, apart from the crowd, and with nothing left that he can do.

The word for one who has nothing, used here with a preposition that makes him needy toward whatever is sent rather than needy in general. That construction is why the sentence names no particular want.
Left deliberately indefinite. This Book uses the word for wealth in some places, but the grammar here keeps it open, so he is asking for whatever comes rather than for a category of thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade was infrastructure. Around a well, the shaded side of a wall or a single tree was where travellers rested, ate and waited out the middle of the day, and the right to sit there was informal and understood. A stranger with no tribe would take the edge of it. That is the physical position the ayah puts him in when he prays.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer is eight words in Arabic and contains no request at all. It states a condition rather than naming a want, and the answer arrives in the very next ayah in the form of a person walking toward him. Commentators often point at this line as an instance of asking by describing where you actually are.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer defines a person by their relation to what is given rather than by what they hold. That is a general claim rather than a description of a hard moment: everyone stands in the same relation, and destitution only makes it visible. Placing it in the mouth of a man who has just done unpaid work for strangers is what keeps it from sounding like self-pity.

crossReferences.why: States the same relation as a general truth: you are the poor toward God, who is the rich.
Gives the answer arriving, in the form of one of the two women coming back.
Sets relief immediately beside hardship, in the same compressed way this passage does.

studies.applyIt: Try praying once this week without asking for anything. Just describe where you actually are, in one accurate sentence, including the part you would normally leave out. Then stop. Most of us move to the request so fast that we never say the true thing, and the true thing is usually shorter than the request was.

studies.title: You Have Escaped Them
studies.meaning: One of the two comes back, walking with a shyness the ayah stops to record, and delivers an invitation framed as a debt: my father is calling you, to pay you for watering for us. Then the scene jumps. He arrives, tells the whole account, and the old man says two things and no more. Do not fear. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people. Commentators note that no advice is given and no judgement is passed on what he has just confessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The word used here for the account Moses gives is the word that names the surah, and this is the one moment in the narrative where a fugitive tells his own history to a stranger. No occasion of revelation is reported. The reception he receives follows the ordinary obligation of hospitality, and the first audience would have recognised the sequence exactly.

keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran, from the root that also gives the word for life. The ayah describes how she walks rather than what she says, which is unusual reporting for this Book.
The word for pay owed for work done. Framing the invitation as a debt rather than as charity is what makes it possible for a man in his position to accept it without shame.
From the root for following a track, and the word that gives this surah its name. He follows his own history through from the beginning, which is what the verb implies.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hospitality to a stranger was the strongest social obligation in the region, and it carried a rule of restraint: you fed a guest before asking his business. What happens here follows that pattern. He is brought in, he tells his story unprompted, and the reply addresses only his safety, because the host's obligation was to shelter him rather than to assess him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing how she walks occurs once in the Quran. It comes from the same root as the word for life, and Arabic treats modesty and vitality as connected in a way English does not. It is one of very few places in the Book where a person's manner of movement is reported at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The rescue promised at the surah's opening arrives here in the plainest possible form: a meal, a wage and an old man saying you are safe. Nothing is announced as providence. And the host's answer models something exact, which is that a person confessing the worst thing they have done is told first that they are safe, before anything else is said to them.

crossReferences.why: Gives the encounter at the well that this invitation is repaying.
Continues the same conversation, with her recommendation that her father hire him.
Shows another man telling his whole account after long separation and danger.

studies.applyIt: The first thing said to a man who has just confessed a killing is that he is safe. Notice what you say first when somebody tells you something difficult about themselves. Most of us reach for a question, or for a comment on the facts. Try beginning, once, with the sentence that tells them nothing bad is about to happen here.

studies.title: The Strong And The Trustworthy
studies.meaning: One of the two makes a recommendation in a single line, and it is an argument rather than a request. Hire him. The best person you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy. She does not say she likes him and she does not narrate what happened at the well. She gives her father a general principle and leaves him to apply it, which commentators read as the reason the recommendation carries.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Hiring outside labour for herding was ordinary in a pastoral economy, and a household with an old man and no sons had a practical problem the previous ayah has already stated. No occasion of revelation is reported. This is the second time in the surah that a young woman's few words change the direction the narrative takes.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from the root for wages. It proposes a working arrangement rather than a favour, which is what allows a stranger with nothing to enter the household without becoming a dependent.
With the definite article, so this names a type rather than a man. She is describing a category of worker, and the listener is left to notice for himself who has just fitted it.
From the root of safety. The pairing of strength with trustworthiness occurs in one other place in the Quran, where a powerful being uses those same two words to recommend himself to a king.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hiring a herdsman meant handing over animals that were a household's entire capital and letting them out of sight for days at a time. Strength kept the flock safe and trustworthiness kept it from being quietly sold. Every family in a pastoral economy had a story about getting one of the two without the other, which is why her sentence needed no explaining.
studies.didYouKnow: The two qualities she names occur together in only one other place in the Quran, where a powerful being from the unseen offers his services to Solomon using exactly these two words about himself. There the pairing is a boast. Here it is an assessment made by an observer, about a man who has said nothing whatever about himself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a woman's judgement of character carry the plot forward, and presents that judgement as reasoning rather than as intuition. She had one afternoon of evidence and built a general criterion out of it. What this surah keeps demonstrating is that its announced outcome travels through people exercising ordinary discernment well, and this is the clearest instance of it.

crossReferences.why: Holds the only other pairing of strong and trustworthy, spoken as a boast before Solomon.
Gives the afternoon at the well on which her entire assessment rests.
Shows another ruler entrusting responsibility to a stranger on the strength of his character.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you recommended someone. Did you say why, in terms the other person could check, or did you mostly say that you liked them? She does the first, in a handful of words, and it is why her father acts. Next time you vouch for somebody, name the two qualities that actually matter for the task.

studies.title: Eight Years, Or Ten
studies.meaning: The old man makes an offer and the terms are unusually careful. He proposes a marriage to one of his two daughters against eight years of work, adds that completing ten would be from Moses' own side, says he does not intend to make things hard, and closes by hoping to be found among the upright. Commentators note the accumulation of qualifications. Every clause after the first exists to reduce the pressure on a man who has nowhere else to go.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arrangements in which labour stood in place of a payment were known across the ancient Near East and would have been intelligible to this surah's audience without any explanation. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The classical commentators discuss its details at length and generally decline to build anything general on a proposal reported inside a narrative.

keyTerms.note: A plural occurring once in the Quran. It is built from the word for pilgrimage, since a year was counted by the return of the season when people travelled, which is how the term came to mean a year.

keyTerms.gloss: to make it hard on you
keyTerms.note: From the root for splitting and for hardship. He raises the possibility of imposing on Moses only in order to deny it, which is a way of naming the imbalance between them out loud.
From the root for what is in good order, the opposite of the word used of Pharaoh in this surah's fourth ayah. He offers himself as something Moses can verify over time rather than assert now.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man with no property could not marry, and a household with no sons could not work its animals. Arrangements that solved both at once were common, and their terms were spoken aloud in front of witnesses rather than written down. The length was the negotiable part. Eight years of a young man's labour was a serious commitment, and the extra two are explicitly left to him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for years occurs once in the Quran. It is built from the same root as the word for pilgrimage, because a year in Arabia was counted by the return of the season in which people travelled to a sanctuary. The unit of time and the journey that measured it shared a single name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The offer is made by the stronger party and drafted to protect the weaker one, which is what the ayah is quietly showing. Nothing compels the old man to leave the last two years optional, or to say aloud that he does not mean to burden his guest, or to submit himself to being judged upright later on. The passage records the position of power and the restraint separately.

crossReferences.why: Gives the recommendation that prompts this offer, made a moment earlier by his daughter.
Records Moses' reply, accepting and stating the terms so neither party can be wronged.
Explains the household's difficulty, which this arrangement is designed to solve.

studies.applyIt: Notice the last time you held the stronger hand in an arrangement: as an employer, a landlord, a parent, someone owed a favour. Did you set the terms at what you could get, or below it? The old man here leaves two whole years to the other man's discretion. Find one term this month that you could leave open in the same way.

studies.title: God Is Witness To This
studies.meaning: Moses accepts, and then does one more thing: he states the terms back. Whichever of the two periods I complete, there is to be no hostility toward me. And God is the one relied upon for what we are saying. Commentators note that he is guarding against a dispute that has not happened, in a household where he has been treated generously. The agreement is closed not by a document but by naming a witness both parties have to answer to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Agreements in that world were oral and held in place by memory, reputation and the presence of witnesses, and quarrels over terms were among the commonest causes of feud. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. Moses is a stranger with no clan in Madyan, which is exactly the position in which an oral agreement is hardest to enforce afterwards.

keyTerms.note: A dual form occurring once in the Quran. Naming both periods rather than choosing between them is the whole of his protection, since it fixes in advance that either would discharge the agreement.
From the root for crossing a limit. He is not guarding against non-payment but against a later claim that he owes more, which is the way an agreement of this kind is usually broken.
The word for someone a matter is entrusted to. Here it makes God the party the agreement is deposited with, which in a culture without documents is the strongest security available.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything was oral. A sale, a marriage, a loan and a term of service were all held together by what witnesses remembered and by what a man's people would do if he broke his word. A stranger had no people. Calling on God over the wording was the one form of security open to someone with no clan behind him, and it was taken seriously.
studies.didYouKnow: The dual form Moses uses for the two possible terms occurs once in the Quran. His entire reply is one sentence in three parts: he restates the choice, he rules out any claim against him afterwards, and he names a witness. Nothing in it concerns the marriage, and nothing in it concerns the wage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Clarity is presented here as compatible with trust rather than opposed to it. He has just been sheltered and fed by this man, and he still states the terms plainly and calls God to witness them, and nothing in the passage treats that as ingratitude. What the ayah models is that an agreement is best made explicit at the moment when both parties still think well of each other.

crossReferences.why: Contains the offer whose terms this reply restates and then closes.
Speaks of fulfilling an undertaking once it is made and God has been set as guarantor.
Says an undertaking will be asked about, which is what naming a witness anticipates.

studies.applyIt: Think of an arrangement you are in that was never quite spelled out: who does what at home, what a favour was actually for, when a loan gets repaid. Pick the one most likely to go wrong. Say the terms out loud to the other person this week, while you still like each other. That is the whole lesson here.

studies.title: A Fire By The Mountain
studies.meaning: Ten years end in half a sentence and the family sets out. He catches sight of a fire on the side of the mountain and tells them to wait, giving two entirely practical reasons: I may bring you news from there, or a burning branch so you can warm yourselves. Commentators note that he expects a camp rather than a revelation. The Arabic verb he uses is not simply seeing; it means glimpsing something with the relief of finding company.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Moses is travelling at night with his household across open country, and a fire in the distance meant people: a camp, directions, and something to carry back. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The same moment is told in two other surahs with slightly different wording, and this version is the only one that mentions warming themselves.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives the words for human beings and for familiarity. It means catching sight of something in a way that suggests other people, which is why it is used of fire at night.
Occurs once in the Quran. It is a piece of wood with fire on one end, the ordinary way of carrying flame from one camp to another before anyone could make a fire quickly.
A verb for drawing close to a fire for its heat. Its presence here, absent from the parallel accounts, gives the scene a temperature: a cold night, a waiting family, a practical errand.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Starting a fire from nothing was slow work, so fire was carried rather than made. A traveller who saw one at night walked toward it for both the reasons Moses names: to ask where he was, and to borrow flame. Refusing either request to a stranger was close to unthinkable. His plan in this ayah is the most ordinary plan a night traveller could have.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing what he saw appears three times in the Quran, in surahs 20 and 27 and here, always of this same night. The word for the burning brand he hopes to bring back occurs only in this version, and so does the detail about warming themselves. Each telling keeps different parts of one errand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The commission that changes everything begins with a man looking for directions and firewood. The passage is unhurried about it, giving his practical reasoning in full before anything at all happens, which places the encounter inside an ordinary night rather than outside one. Nothing about his intention is religious, and nothing in the account suggests it needed to be.

crossReferences.why: Tells the same night with the same verb, and a longer list of what he hoped to find.
Gives the briefest version of this moment, a few lines before the fire speaks.
Continues immediately, with what he found when he reached the fire.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last major turn in your life and where you were going when it happened. Most people were on an errand. This ayah spends its length on the errand rather than on the fire, which is a way of saying that the ordinary walk toward something small is where the rest of it usually begins.

studies.title: Called From The Bush
studies.meaning: The call arrives with an address that names four things: the side of the valley, its right-hand side, a blessed patch of ground, and the tree. Then the words themselves, which are the shortest possible self-identification. It is I, God, Lord of the Worlds. Commentators note how much of the ayah is location and how little is content. The place is described in detail; the speaker states who He is and nothing more.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The site is named with unusual precision for a Book that rarely gives geography. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The parallel accounts in surahs 20 and 27 set the same event down without this detail, and the classical commentators note that this version is the one which fixes the ground itself as blessed.

keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran. It is the edge of a valley or a watercourse, so the location is given the way a local would give it, by the feature you would be standing beside.
Occurs once in the Quran. It means a specific piece of earth distinguished from what surrounds it, which is why the adjective that follows attaches to the ground rather than to the event.
The phrase that opens the Quran's first surah. Its scope is the point here: a voice at one bush in one valley identifies itself by everything, and not by the place it happens to be speaking from.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Holiness attached to places all over Arabia. Particular valleys, trees and stones were treated as sacred, tended by families and visited for oaths and requests. An audience hearing that a patch of ground was blessed would have recognised the category at once. What would have struck them is that the blessing is announced by the speaker, and that nothing is said about tending the site afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the one for the valley's bank and the one for the patch of blessed ground. Both are terms of location. The surah spends its rarest vocabulary on saying exactly where he was standing, while the message itself uses one of the most familiar phrases in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The self-identification is deliberately minimal. No attribute is offered, no demand is attached in the same breath, and the title given is the widest available. Setting that at a particular bush in a particular valley holds together two things religion often separates: an encounter that happened somewhere exact, and a speaker whose relation to everywhere else is unaltered by it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same call with more words, including the instruction about his sandals.
Reports the same voice with a different opening, blessing whoever is at the fire.
Opens the Quran with the same title the voice uses to identify itself here.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much detail you keep about where you were when something important was said to you: the room, the light, what you were holding. That is not sentimentality; it is how people actually store the things that changed them. Write down the location of one such moment today, in the plain way this ayah does it.

studies.title: Come Forward, Do Not Fear
studies.meaning: The staff is thrown down and it moves like a fast snake, and Moses turns and runs without looking back. The ayah records the fear plainly. Then the voice does three things in order: it calls him by name, tells him to come forward, and tells him he is among the secure. Commentators note that the fear is not rebuked anywhere. It is answered with an instruction to approach and a statement of fact about his safety.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The scene is told in three surahs, and this version is the briefest on the sign and the fullest on the reassurance. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The audience were people being prepared for work most of them expected to be dangerous, and the sequence here, fear followed by an instruction to come nearer, would have carried its own weight.

keyTerms.note: A verb for quick continuous motion, used elsewhere of the earth stirring after rain. It describes movement rather than shape, which is why the comparison that follows it is needed at all.
A word for a small fast snake, sharing a root with the word for the unseen beings. The comparison is about speed, since a small snake moves far faster than a large one.
From the root of safety and of trust. The reassurance names a group rather than a feeling, so he is told what his position is rather than told to calm himself down.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Snakes were an everyday hazard rather than a symbol. People slept on the ground, stored grain where mice came, and knew that the small quick ones were the dangerous ones. Running without looking back was the correct response and not a failure of nerve. Anybody in the first audience would have done exactly what the ayah describes him doing.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase comparing the staff to a swift serpent appears twice in the Quran, here and in the surah immediately before this one, in identical wording. Those two surahs sit side by side, both open with the same letters, and both tell this scene, and this is one of the few sentences they share word for word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is treated as information rather than as a fault. The man being appointed here has just run from something, and the appointment continues without a pause. What is offered is not courage but a fact about his standing, and he is asked to act on the fact while the feeling is still present, which is a considerable amount of realism inside three short clauses.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical sentence about the staff, in the surah immediately before this one.
Tells the same moment and adds the instruction to take hold of it again.
Shows the same staff thrown down before Pharaoh's court, where it becomes a plain serpent.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you avoid because your body reacts before you have decided anything: a phone call, a room, a conversation. The instruction here is not to stop being afraid. It is to come forward while afraid, on the strength of something you have been told rather than something you feel. Do one small version of that today.

studies.title: Two Proofs And One Fear
studies.meaning: Two signs are given, and then the destination is named: Pharaoh and his court. A hand drawn out white and unblemished, and an arm pressed to the side against fear. They are called two conclusive proofs. Then Moses answers, and his answer is not about the signs at all. I killed one of them, and I fear they will kill me. Commentators note that the objection is practical rather than theological, and that it is left standing until the following ayah.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The killing described earlier in this same surah is what Moses now raises, which is one reason the surah told that episode at such length. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The audience were being asked to carry a message to people who already had personal reasons to be hostile to them, and this sequence would not have felt abstract.

keyTerms.note: A verb for threading something into a narrow place. This exact instruction occurs once in the Quran; the parallel accounts use the ordinary verb for entering instead of this one.
Occurs in this sense only here. The instruction to press the arm to the side against it treats fear as something with a bodily remedy, which the commentators discuss at some length.
The dual of the word for decisive evidence. Calling the signs proofs rather than wonders defines what they are for: they are addressed to a court and intended to settle a question.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger between rulers carried tokens: a seal, a garment, a phrase agreed beforehand. Nobody was admitted to a court on their word alone, and every listener understood that a claim of authority needed something visible attached to it. What Moses is given fits that pattern exactly, and his objection is the objection of a man who knows what will actually be discussed in the room.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for putting his hand inside his garment occurs once in the Quran. The word for the fear he is told to press his arm against also occurs in this sense only here. The two rarest words in the passage describe a gesture rather than a miracle, and the commentaries give the gesture more space than the hand.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Signs are given, and they do not remove the difficulty. Moses immediately raises an ordinary human obstacle, a killing and its likely consequence, and the passage lets it stand for a whole ayah without correcting him. That says something about the relationship being described. The equipping is real, and it does not include removing a reasonable fear or a past that is still owed.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same two signs in the surah before this one, using the ordinary verb for entering.
Repeats the sign of the hand and calls it another sign, in a shorter form.
Records the killing that Moses raises here as his objection to being sent.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you actually say when someone asks you to do something you are qualified for. Most people do not argue about ability; they raise the past, or a particular person who will be in the room. Say that objection out loud once this week to somebody, instead of using it silently as a reason not to begin.

studies.title: My Brother Is More Eloquent
studies.meaning: The second objection is about capability and it is stated without embarrassment. My brother Aaron is clearer of speech than I am, so send him with me as a support, to confirm me. Then the reason: I fear they will call me a liar. Commentators note that the request is for corroboration rather than for a spokesman. He does not ask to be spared the task; he asks for a second voice, because a single claim is easy to dismiss.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had by this point been calling for years and had been accused of every kind of fabrication, and the objection Moses raises here, that one man's report will simply be denied, was a live matter for the surah's first hearers. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah itself.

keyTerms.note: A comparative occurring once in the Quran, from a root meaning to speak plainly without impediment. It later gave Arabic its entire vocabulary for eloquence, and here it is one brother comparing himself with another.
Occurs once in the Quran. It names something propped behind another thing to keep it standing, so the request is for reinforcement rather than for a replacement or a substitute voice.
A verb for declaring someone's report true. What is being asked for is corroboration, which is a matter of evidence rather than of eloquence, and is the real content of the request.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A single witness settled nothing. In a dispute a claim was carried by the number and standing of the people prepared to affirm it, and a man with nobody to confirm his account stood in a weak position no matter how true it was. Asking for a brother who would confirm him was asking for the ordinary minimum a claim needed in order to be heard at all.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this short ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the comparative for clearer speech, and the noun for a support propped behind something. The root of the first went on to name the standard register of the Arabic language itself, and its only appearance in the Book is a man saying somebody else has more of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prophet states a limitation about himself and asks for help, and the request is granted in full in the next ayah. Nothing suggests that needing assistance is a defect to be overcome. The passage presents the task as larger than one person deliberately, and it lets the person appointed be the one who notices that first, which is a particular view of what being chosen involves.

crossReferences.why: Gives the fuller version of this request, including the untying of a knot from his tongue.
Records the same fears in another surah, with the chest tightening and the tongue not loosening.
Contains the answer, granting the brother and adding something he had not asked for.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you are worst at in a role you hold, out loud, to one person who works with you. Not as an apology. As a fact, followed by what you would like instead. Moses does this in one sentence and asks for a specific person. Most of us conceal the gap and then work twice as hard around it.

studies.title: We Will Strengthen Your Arm
studies.meaning: The answer grants the request and then goes past it. We will strengthen your arm with your brother, and give you both an authority, so they will not reach you.
