Then a promise in the plural that takes in people not yet present: you two and whoever follows you are the ones who prevail. Commentators note the shift. What was asked for was a witness; what is given is a pairing, a protection, and an outcome covering everyone who joins them later.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The promise that they would not be reached had an obvious application for a community that was being reached regularly, and the surah does not draw it out. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The classical commentators read the final clause as covering the followers of both brothers rather than only the two men, since the wording widens deliberately.

keyTerms.note: The part of the arm between shoulder and elbow, where strength is felt. It occurs once in the Quran, and Arabic uses it as an idiom for the support that makes a person able to act at all.
A word covering both power and the evidence that justifies it. Commentators read it here as the standing that comes from carrying real proof, rather than as force of any kind.
A definite plural, so it names a group rather than predicting a single event. Its scope widens in the same clause to include those who follow, which makes the promise outlast the two men.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The upper arm was where a listener located strength. Poets praised a chief by his arm, and saying that someone strengthened your arm meant they made your action possible rather than that they helped from time to time. The idiom survives in Arabic still. It named the person you could not do the work without, which is exactly what is being granted here.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the upper arm occurs once in the Quran, in this promise. A related form appears in one other place, where God says He did not take those who mislead as a support. The same anatomical image is used once for what is granted to Moses and once for what is refused to anybody else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What is asked for is granted and then enlarged in the same breath, in a direction the asker had not considered. He wanted his account confirmed; he is given a partner, a warrant, and an assurance about everyone who will ever follow him. The passage keeps the granting recognisably an answer to the request while making the response larger than the fear that produced it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same request granted in the parallel account, item by item.
Contains the request this ayah answers, and shows how much wider the answer runs.
States the same outcome as a general decree, that God and His messengers prevail.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person who makes your work possible rather than merely easier: the one whose absence would stop it, not slow it. Most people have one and have never said so. Tell them this week, in a sentence that names what specifically they make possible. The idiom in this ayah is about exactly that person.

studies.title: Fabricated Magic, They Said
studies.meaning: The signs arrive clear, and the reply is two objections that do not fit together. This is nothing but invented sorcery, and we never heard of this among our earliest fathers. The first says the thing is a trick; the second says it is unprecedented. Commentators note that the second is the real one. A claim that something was never done before is not an argument about truth, and the passage lets the pair stand without comment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The identical two objections were being made in Mecca while this surah was being recited, in the same order and often in the same breath. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. Setting the pair in an Egyptian court centuries earlier let the audience hear their own reasoning without being addressed by it, which is one of this surah's methods throughout.

keyTerms.note: A plural adjective attached to the signs before the reply is quoted. The ayah settles the question of clarity in advance, so the objection that follows cannot be about evidence being hard to read.
From the root for inventing a lie. Attaching it to sorcery makes a double charge: not merely magic but magic concocted, which was the standard way of dismissing anything that could not be matched.
The appeal to precedent, which appears in this Book as the most persistent objection of all. It says nothing about whether a thing is true and everything about whether it is familiar.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sorcery was a working profession with recognised practitioners and a going rate. Calling something sorcery was not a wild accusation; it named a category people knew, and it explained an effect without conceding its source. It also carried a practical implication, that a sorcerer could be beaten by a better one, which is what Pharaoh's court attempts shortly afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for invented sorcery occurs once in the Quran. The second objection, that they had never heard of such a thing among their earliest ancestors, is one of the most repeated dismissals in the whole Book, and it is almost always given in the objectors' own words rather than summarised by the narration.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets clarity and rejection side by side and refuses to treat the second as a failure of the first. The signs were plain; the reply was ready-made. What is being described is a mode of response that does not examine, and the two objections quoted expose it, since a thing cannot both be a trick you have seen through and something nobody has ever heard of.

crossReferences.why: Gives the appeal to ancestral practice in its plainest form, as the whole of an answer.
Records the same charge of sorcery against these same signs, along with Moses' reply.
Shows the objection shifting later, when a second scripture is dismissed for a new reason.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the two objections inside your own dismissals: that is a trick, and nobody I know does that. They cannot both be doing work at once. When you next reject something quickly, check which of the two you actually mean, and whether the second is an argument or only a description of your habits.

studies.title: Who Brings Guidance From Him
studies.meaning: Moses does not answer the charge. He says his Lord knows better who has come with guidance from Him and who will have the final home, and then adds one flat statement: wrongdoers do not succeed. Commentators read this as a refusal to argue rather than a failure to answer. He transfers the question to a judge, names the criterion it will be settled by, and stops, leaving the court holding an accusation nobody has taken up.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the same stretch as the objections in the ayah before it. No occasion of revelation is reported. The phrase about the final home appears once more in the Quran, in another Meccan passage answering the same kind of challenge. Replying to a mocking charge by naming who will decide it belongs to this whole period of the message.

keyTerms.note: A comparative used absolutely. It does not claim that Moses knows and they do not; it says the matter is known by someone else entirely, which removes the dispute from the room.
Literally what follows for the abode. The phrase occurs twice in the Quran and both times answers a challenge, pointing at how things end rather than at how they look at present.
From a root meaning to split the ground for planting. Success in this Book carries agricultural imagery: something opened up and yielding, rather than something seized or won.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public disputes were won by the last speaker and the loudest crowd, and a man who declined to trade insults was usually taken to have lost. Poets built entire reputations on exchanges of this kind. Answering a court's mockery by referring the matter elsewhere would have struck that audience as an unusual move, and its strangeness is part of why it is recorded.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah, that wrongdoers do not succeed, appears word for word at the end of an ayah in surah 6, which also carries the same phrase about the final home. There the words are given to the Prophet to say to his own opponents. At that point Moses' reply and his are one sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply relocates the argument rather than winning it. Two questions are named, who came with guidance and who ends well, and both are handed to the one who knows, which leaves the accusation deliberately unanswered. What follows is not a threat but a rule: wrongdoing does not come out well. The passage treats that as a fact about how things run rather than as a prediction.

crossReferences.why: Ends with the identical clause and uses the same phrase about the final home.
Gives the same form of reply again: work as you are, and you will come to know.
Closes another Moses passage by telling the objectors to wait and see who is guided.

studies.applyIt: Next time you are accused of something in front of other people, notice the pull to win the exchange. Try, once, saying only what you actually believe and then stopping. Not silence, and not a counter-charge. One sentence, and then let the room hold it. It is uncomfortable, and it changes what happens next.

studies.title: Build Me A Tower
studies.meaning: Pharaoh addresses his court with a claim and an order. I know of no god for you other than myself; so fire the kilns over the clay and build me a tower, and I will climb up and look for the God of Moses. Then the aside: I think he is lying. Commentators note the incoherence the ayah records. A man who has just announced there is no other god commissions a building project in order to go and inspect one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The speech is repeated in almost identical wording in surah 40, so it was given twice in the recitation. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. Its first audience lived in a city whose leaders both maintained a sanctuary and dismissed a message about one God, a combination beside which this contradiction would not have felt unfamiliar.

keyTerms.note: The verb for lighting a fire, applied here to firing clay. The instruction is technical: bricks had to be baked before they could carry anything like the height he is describing.
The same word used in the surah before this one for the glass floored hall a visiting queen mistook for water. There it exposed an illusion; here it is commissioned in order to disprove God.

keyTerms.gloss: that I may look up at
keyTerms.note: A verb for peering over an edge or into something from above. It treats the God of Moses as an object that could be located from sufficient height, which is what the sentence exposes.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia built in stone and mud brick and had nothing on the scale being described here. Traders who had seen Mesopotamian and Egyptian construction brought back accounts of towers that Arabian audiences found genuinely hard to picture. Pharaoh's order would have registered as the boast of a man with resources beyond anything the listeners commanded, which is part of why it is quoted in full.
studies.didYouKnow: The order to build this tower appears twice in the Quran, here and in surah 40, in almost the same words. The word used for the structure occurs in only one other passage, in the surah immediately before this one, where it names the glass floor that revealed a queen's mistake rather than a king's.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech is left to convict itself. A claim to be the only god is followed immediately by a plan to go looking for another one, and the passage adds no comment at all. What is being exhibited is not stupidity but the shape of a certain kind of denial, which asserts confidently and then quietly hedges, and would rather build something enormous than examine a claim it has already dismissed.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same order in almost identical words, with the outcome added afterwards.
Uses the same word for a structure, there a glass floor that exposed a mistake.
Records the other claim attributed to him, that he was the highest lord.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the sentence in which you dismiss something and then immediately act as though it might be true: the offer you called worthless and then checked twice, the warning you laughed at and then looked up. Notice one this week. The gap between what you say and what you do is usually where your real estimate lives.

studies.title: They Thought They Would Not Return
studies.meaning: Two lines close the Egyptian narrative. He and his forces were arrogant in the land without right, and they supposed they would not be returned to Us. Then the seizure, given in a single verb, and the throwing into the water. The reader is told to look at the outcome. Commentators note where the ayah locates the root: not in cruelty, and not in the claim to divinity, but in an assumption about what happens afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The whole account has been running since the surah's fourth ayah and it ends here in two lines, with no description of the crossing, the pursuit or the parting of the water. No occasion of revelation is reported. Other surahs give those events at length, so the compression is a choice: this version keeps the political analysis and drops the spectacle.

keyTerms.note: A verb for making oneself great, from the same root used of the refusal to bow at the beginning of the human story. It describes a posture adopted rather than a status actually held.
A verb covering both opinion and conviction. It marks the belief about never being returned as an assumption rather than a doctrine, which is how such beliefs usually operate in practice.
A verb for tossing something aside as worthless, used elsewhere of discarding a covenant behind the back. Applying it to an army is deliberate, and the same word describes another destroyed people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drowning was a particular horror for a people who mostly did not swim. Red Sea trade was coastal, and Arabian audiences knew wrecks as total losses, bodies and cargo alike gone without recovery or burial. The verb used here, for throwing something away, describes exactly what the sea did with things in the imagination of people who lived beside it.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for what happened to Pharaoh's forces appears in this form twice in the Quran. The other is in surah 51, of a different people seized and cast into the sea. It is a word for discarding something as worthless, and the Quran uses the same root elsewhere for a covenant thrown behind the back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies the operative belief and places it before the acts. What made the arrogance possible was an assumption that nothing would ever be returned to anyone, which is a claim about accountability rather than about theology. That relocates the argument the whole surah has been making. Whether there is a reckoning turns out to shape how a man behaves in a room long before it settles anything else.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for another people seized and flung into the sea.
Gives the drowning at length, including what he said as the water closed over him.
States the policy this outcome answers, at the opening of the same narrative.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you would do differently this week if you were certain every conversation would be replayed to you accurately. Not judged, just replayed. This passage names an assumption rather than a cruelty as the root of what followed. Most people's worst behaviour rests on a quiet confidence that nobody is keeping the record.

studies.title: Leaders Calling To The Fire
studies.meaning: The verdict on Pharaoh's line is given in a phrase that inverts the surah's own vocabulary. Earlier the weakened were to be made leaders; here the rulers are made leaders too, calling toward the Fire. Then two clauses about the Day: no help will reach them, and they will be among the disfigured. Commentators note that the word used for their state occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and that it describes a collapse of standing rather than of the body.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the drowning. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The surah is speaking to people who could see leadership exercised in front of them every day by men whose position looked permanent, and the passage supplies the long view of what such leadership is doing rather than any prediction about particular individuals.

keyTerms.note: The word for those placed in front to be followed. This surah uses it twice: once of the weakened who were to be raised, and once here of the rulers, so one office runs in two directions.
From a root meaning to drive off. It is less a spoken imprecation than a distance imposed, and the ayah says it followed them through this world rather than waiting for the next.
Occurs once in the Quran, from a root for what is ugly to look at. Commentators read it of a loss of standing made visible, the exact opposite of the elevation these men spent their lives on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour was visible. A man's standing showed in where he sat, who greeted him first, and how his name was spoken when he was absent, and losing it was a public event the whole settlement could observe. To be called disfigured in that world was not a statement about appearance. It described someone whose position had collapsed in front of people who had known him.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for their condition on the Day occurs once in the whole Quran, here. The word used for leaders in the same passage occurs twice in this surah: once at the very beginning, promising that the oppressed would be made leaders, and once here. The same title is given to both parties in one story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Leadership is treated as a direction rather than as a rank. Both the persecuted and the persecutors are named with the same word, and what separates them is where they are leading, which makes the office itself neutral and the destination the whole question. That is a demanding way to read authority, because it applies to anyone others actually follow, whatever they are called.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for leaders, promising it to the very people being crushed here.
Describes another leader going before his people and bringing them to the Fire.
Gives the other use of the word, of leaders guiding by God's own command.

studies.applyIt: You lead somebody, whether or not it is your title: a younger sibling, a team, a group chat that takes its tone from you. Ask where the following you actually have is heading. Not what you say, and not what you intend. Just the direction people move in after an hour in your company.

studies.title: You Were Not There
studies.meaning: The Book given to Moses is described in three words, insights for people, guidance and mercy, and dated after the destruction of earlier generations. Then the surah turns and states a fact: you were not on the western side when the command was decreed, and you were not among the witnesses. Commentators read the second ayah as an argument rather than a remark. The account just given could not have come from memory or from having been present.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge that the recitation had been learned from somewhere is answered here without ever being quoted. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. Three such statements follow one after another over the next few lines, each naming a place the Prophet was not: the western side, the households of Madyan, and the side of the mountain.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for inner sight rather than eyesight. It appears five times in the Quran, and it describes what a text does for a reader rather than what the text happens to contain.
A word for a span of people living at one time, and by extension for an age. Dating the Book by communities already gone sets it inside a sequence rather than at any beginning.

Occurs once in the Quran. It names the side of a valley by compass direction, a level of geographical detail this Book almost never gives, and it is given in order to say the hearer was not standing there.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An account's authority came from its chain of transmission. Who told you, and who told them, and were they present. Arabian audiences were expert in this kind of assessment because it was how poetry, genealogy and news all travelled. A narrative full of detail with no chain attached would immediately prompt the question the next ayat are answering.
studies.didYouKnow: The word naming the western side occurs once in the Quran. It is one of very few compass directions the Book uses of a physical place at all, and it is used in order to state that the person being addressed was not there. The precision is spent on a denial rather than on a description.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs by exclusion. The account is detailed, and the one reciting it was not present, had no informant among the people involved, and lived centuries later in another country. What follows is that the detail must have come from somewhere else, and the surah leaves that inference to the reader rather than stating it, which is why the denials are simply listed.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same series of denials, naming another place he was not present.
Makes the same argument about Joseph's story, that he was not with them when they schemed.
Says the same of Mary's account, that he was not there when the lots were cast.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you are certain about you were never present for. Almost everything, in fact: the history of your family, your country, your own first two years. We accept transmitted knowledge constantly and only interrogate it when we dislike the conclusion. Pick one belief this week and ask honestly how you came by it.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Time Grew Long Over Them
studies.meaning: Between Moses and the present, one sentence about the interval. We brought generations into being, and the span of years stretched out over them. Then a second denial: nor were you resident among the people of Madyan, reciting Our signs to them. The ayah closes with three words that answer the whole objection: but We were sending messengers. Commentators note the two halves. One explains why a reminder was needed at all, and the other explains where it came from.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The gap between Moses and the seventh century was real and the surah does not minimise it, describing the intervening period as time doing its ordinary work on memory. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The mention of Madyan matters because this surah has just told a long Madyan episode nobody in Arabia had heard in that form.

keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran. A verb for something extending over time until it wearies, so the clause describes duration wearing a memory down rather than any single act of forgetting.
Occurs once in the Quran. It means settled in a place for a period rather than passing through, which is exactly the kind of stay that would explain knowing local detail about it.
An active participle, so the clause names an ongoing practice rather than a single dispatch. It answers the whole objection, compressed into three words at the very end of the ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Memory in an oral culture was carefully maintained and still had limits. Genealogies were kept for many generations and poetry preserved names and battles, but detail decayed at a known rate, and everyone understood that a story four centuries old arrived changed. The ayah describes something its first audience could measure against their own family histories.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the verb for time stretching out over people, and the word for being resident in a place. Both concern duration in one location. The sentence spends its rarest vocabulary describing exactly the two ways a person could have come by this knowledge honestly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgetting is described here without blame, as something time does. That matters for what follows, because it makes the sending of messengers a response to an ordinary process rather than to any special wickedness. The final clause states the practice in the plural and in the continuous, which places this recitation inside a long habit rather than presenting it as an interruption of one.

crossReferences.why: Warns against the same process, hearts hardening because the interval had grown long.
Speaks of a messenger arriving after a gap in the succession of messengers.
Gives the third denial in the series, and names the purpose behind the sending.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you knew clearly ten years ago and can no longer reconstruct: a phone number, a face, why a friendship ended. Nothing went wrong. Time did what it does. Now notice which of the things you care about you have never written down anywhere, and write one of them down this week.

studies.title: A Mercy From Your Lord
studies.meaning: The third denial completes the set: nor were you at the side of the mountain when We called out. Then the correction, and a single word carries it. Rather, it is a mercy from your Lord. What follows names the purpose, to warn a people to whom no warner had come before. Commentators note that the account is not explained as an achievement or as a reward, and that the word chosen leaves nothing on the receiving side to have earned it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The statement that no warner had come to this people before described the Arabian situation as the audience themselves understood it: they had heard of scriptures given to others and had none in their own language. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The three denials that close here answer the accusation of borrowing without ever quoting it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for calling across a distance, the same one used earlier in this surah of the voice from the tree. Its use here compresses that whole scene into one word the reader has already met.
In the accusative, so it functions as a reason: this happened as a mercy. The grammar makes it the explanation for the recitation rather than a description of what the recitation contains.
One who gives notice in advance. The word defines a role by timing rather than by content, which is why the ayah can say a people never had one without saying they had never heard anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia knew it was outside the story. Jewish and Christian communities to the north and south had books, scholars and a recorded history, and Arabs trading with them heard about it constantly. Poetry from the period shows an awareness of being a people without a scripture in their own tongue. The clause about no warner coming before names something the audience already felt.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the third of three denials in as many ayat, each naming a place the person addressed was not present: the western side of the valley, the households of Madyan, and the side of the mountain. Between them the three cover the whole Moses narrative this surah has just told, from the flight to the commission.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage refuses two explanations at once. The account did not come from presence, and it did not come from living among people who remembered it. What replaces them is not a claim of merit but a word for unearned favour, and the purpose given afterwards is directed at other people entirely. The recipient is described as a route rather than as a destination.

crossReferences.why: Opens the series of denials, with the first place he was not present.
Repeats that this people had received no warner before, as the reason for sending.
Describes the entire sending as a mercy, using the same word for a wider scope.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you have that you did nothing to deserve: a language, a stable childhood, someone who taught you to read. The structure of this ayah is worth borrowing. Name the thing, then name who it is actually for, since almost nothing given to a person stops with them. Say both halves out loud once.

studies.title: So They Could Not Say That
studies.meaning: One long conditional explains why a messenger was sent at all. If trouble reached them because of what their own hands had sent ahead, they would say: our Lord, if only You had sent us a messenger, we would have followed Your signs and been believers. The sentence never completes its main clause. Commentators supply it as the reason for the sending, and note that the excuse being headed off is one the passage treats as genuinely available.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, immediately after the statement that no warner had come to this people before. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The audience were people who had, until recently, stood in exactly the position the sentence describes: aware of scriptures given to others, with none addressed to them, and able to say so plainly.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to hit a target. The word carries the sense of something arriving accurately rather than at random, which is why it is joined here to what their own hands sent ahead.
A verb for dispatching something in advance of yourself. This Book uses it repeatedly of deeds, picturing them as arriving at a destination before the person who did them gets there.
A particle used to introduce an unmet condition or a reproach. It appears twice in this one ayah, first framing the argument and then inside the excuse itself, which is a deliberate echo.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian practice worked on notice. A tribe did not attack without a declaration, a debt was not enforced without a demand, and blood was not claimed without a formal statement to the family. Moving against someone who had not been told was considered dishonourable rather than merely irregular. The logic of this ayah would have read as ordinary fairness to that audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence has no main clause. Arabic allows a conditional to stand with its answer unstated when that answer is obvious, and the classical commentators supply it the same way: were it not for this, We would not have sent you. It is one of several places where the Quran leaves the load-bearing clause unspoken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds the sending of messengers in something like fairness rather than in generosity, and does so by taking a human objection seriously enough to build its answer around it. Nobody is to be answerable for a message they never received. That places a real constraint inside the account, and it explains prophecy as the removal of an excuse rather than as a display of power.

crossReferences.why: Puts almost the same excuse in the same conditional form, in another Meccan passage.
States the purpose directly, that people have no argument left after messengers come.
Says no community is dealt with until a messenger has been sent to it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a standard you hold someone to that you have never actually told them about: a colleague, a partner, a friend who keeps getting it wrong. Say it once, plainly, this week. Most private disappointment is a rule enforced without notice, and this ayah is about how unfair that arrangement is.

studies.title: Two Works Of Magic
studies.meaning: The truth arrives and the objection is that it came in the wrong format: why was he not given the like of what Moses was given. The reply is a question about their own record. Did they not reject what Moses was given, when it came? Then the position shifts twice more in one line: two sorceries backing each other, and we reject both. Commentators note that the demand and the dismissal cancel out, and the ayah simply records the sequence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Meccan objectors did appeal to the earlier scriptures as a standard, and the reply here turns that appeal against itself. No occasion of revelation is reported. Commentators differ over which two things are being called sorceries in the phrase quoted and record the readings without settling, since the ayah's point does not depend on which pair is meant.

keyTerms.note: The demand is not for evidence but for a matching format. The word asks for the same kind of thing rather than for something convincing, which is why the reply addresses their record instead.
A dual form occurring once in the Quran. Applying it to two scriptures at once is what makes the charge self-defeating, since it discards the very standard the previous sentence appealed to.
From the word for the back, the same root used earlier in this surah for a supporter. Here it accuses two revelations of propping each other up, which quietly concedes that they agree.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan traders had enough contact with Jewish and Christian communities to know that scripture existed and roughly what it looked like. That knowledge was used both ways: as grounds for expecting something similar, and as material for objections when what arrived did not match. This exchange is a snapshot of an argument running in the city continuously.
studies.didYouKnow: The dual form calling two revelations sorcery occurs once in the Quran. The verb attached to it, saying they back one another, comes from the same root as the word for a supporter that Moses uses earlier in this very surah, when he vows never again to be a backer of the guilty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage exposes a pattern rather than refuting a claim. A standard is invoked, and when something meets it the standard is discarded, and the discarding is quoted in the objectors' own words. What the ayah demonstrates is that the demand was never a condition. That is why the answer in the next lines is not more evidence but an invitation to produce a better book.

crossReferences.why: Gives the reply, inviting them to bring a scripture more guiding than either one.
Records the same demand for a matching format, phrased as wanting what messengers received.
Lists further conditions demanded before belief, none of which would have settled it.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you say you would change your mind if only you had a particular kind of proof. Write down what that proof would actually be, in a sentence specific enough that you could recognise it if it arrived. If you cannot, the condition was never a condition, and it is better to know that than to keep announcing it.

studies.title: Then Bring A Better Book
studies.meaning: The answer to the double dismissal is an invitation. Bring a scripture from God more guiding than these two, and I will follow it. Then the next ayah sets out what silence would mean: if they do not respond, they are following their own inclinations, and nobody is further astray than a person following an inclination with no guidance. Commentators note that the offer is genuine in form, and that the second ayah names what a refusal to take it up reveals.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The challenge belongs to a wider pattern in this period, where objectors are repeatedly invited to produce something comparable rather than argued with. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat. The audience were people for whom producing a rival text was a live ambition, since Arabic composition was the accomplishment their culture prized above all others.

keyTerms.note: A comparative, so the criterion offered is usefulness rather than authorship or origin. What is asked for is not a different book but one that does the same job better, which is a testable standard.
The plural of a word whose root means falling. It names not appetite but whatever a person leans toward, which is why this Book contrasts it with guidance rather than with restraint.
The comparative of straying. The ayah does not call following inclination wicked; it calls it directionless, which is a different charge and the one the imagery of the root actually supports.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was judged in public and by comparison. Odes were recited at fairs and gatherings, and audiences ranked them out loud, so a challenge to produce something better was a familiar and serious form of contest. Issuing that challenge about a text was speaking the one competitive language every Arabian listener understood immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for what people follow instead of guidance comes from a root meaning to fall. Arabic builds from that root the words for air, for a chasm, and for love that overtakes a person. The picture of desire is therefore not heat or hunger but descent: something you go along with because it is downhill.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a testable standard and then interprets a failure to meet it. That is a strong move, and its strength depends on the criterion being one anybody can apply: which book guides better. What the second ayah adds is a description rather than a punishment. A person who will not test their position and will not leave it is being led by something, and the ayah names it.

crossReferences.why: Issues the parallel challenge, to produce a single surah like this one.
Describes someone who takes his own inclination as the god he serves.
Contains the double dismissal that this invitation is answering.

studies.applyIt: Pick a position you hold that you have never tested against a serious alternative. Read one good argument for the other side this week, all the way through, without composing your reply as you go. You are allowed to end up where you started. The exercise is about whether you can still be moved, not about being moved.

studies.title: They Said We Already Believed
studies.meaning: One line describes the method: We have joined the message together for them, link after link, so they might remember. Then a group is named, people given a scripture before this one, who believe in it. Their words are quoted: we have believed in it, it is the truth from our Lord, we were submitting before it came. Commentators note that the passage describes recognition rather than persuasion, and that the speakers are not identified beyond what they say.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Individuals from Jewish and Christian communities did respond to the recitation during this period, and the classical sources record several accounts with differing details. No occasion of revelation is reported for these ayat with any consensus. What the passage supplies is the shape of the response rather than the name of anyone giving it.

keyTerms.gloss: We joined it link by link
keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for connecting, occurring once in the Quran in this form. It describes a message delivered in connected instalments rather than all at once, which is how this Book arrived.
The plainest available noun for what is said. Using it rather than a term for scripture keeps the weight on the manner of delivery, which is what the verb before it is describing.
From the root of surrender. The speakers apply the word to themselves before the recitation reached them, so it describes a posture rather than membership of a community formed later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Recognition worked by ear. In a world where texts were heard rather than read, a person who knew one scripture well could tell within a few lines whether a new recitation belonged to the same family of speech. The response quoted here is the response of people who identified something, rather than of people talked round by an argument.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing how the message was delivered occurs once in the Quran in this form. It comes from the root for joining one thing to another, and it pictures the recitation as arriving in linked instalments across years rather than as a single deposited book, which is in fact how it came.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belief is described here as continuity rather than as rupture. The people quoted do not say they have changed; they say they recognise it, and that they were already in this posture. That claim runs in both directions, since it makes the new recitation a continuation rather than a replacement, and the earlier scripture a preparation rather than a rival.

crossReferences.why: Describes people of earlier scripture who believe, humbled before God rather than trading verses.
Records the same recognition, with eyes overflowing at what they knew to be true.
Continues immediately, naming what such people are given and what they do.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time somebody put into words something you had felt for years without being able to say it. That is the experience these ayat describe, and it is not the same as being persuaded. Notice this week what you already half know and have never articulated, and try writing one sentence of it down.

studies.title: Given Their Reward Twice
studies.meaning: Three things are said about the group just described. They are given their reward twice over, because of what they bore; they push away the bad with the good; and they give out of what they have been provided. Commentators note that the first clause gives endurance as the reason rather than membership of two communities, and that the second uses a verb of warding off, so the good deed is described as a defence rather than as a payment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Anyone from a settled religious community who accepted the recitation in this period stood to lose on both sides, from their own people and from the Meccan leadership. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah. The word for what they bore points at that particular cost rather than at hardship in general, and the commentators generally read it that way.

keyTerms.note: A dual, so the doubling is exact rather than a vague increase. The phrase occurs once in the Quran, and the reason attached to it is what these people endured rather than what they belonged to.
A verb for pushing back something coming at you. It occurs twice in the Quran and both times describes meeting a wrong with a good act, presented as a defence rather than as forgiveness.
From a root for something being used up or running through. The usual word for giving in this Book is a word for expenditure, which keeps the act ordinary rather than ceremonial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving your community's religion in that world meant leaving its protection, its marriages and often its trade. There was no neutral ground to stand on and no institution to appeal to. The endurance this ayah names would have been visible to everybody: a person going on living in a place where their standing had quietly collapsed around them.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for warding off a bad thing with a good one occurs twice in the Quran, here and in surah 13, where it stands in a list of what people of understanding do. Both times the good deed is described as repelling something rather than as repaying it, which is an unusual way to picture kindness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The doubled reward is attached to what was borne rather than to what was believed, which keeps the passage from reading as a claim about categories of people. And the second quality is practical: harm is met with a good act because that is what stops it, not because the person happens to feel forgiving. The passage describes a way of behaving available before any feeling arrives.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other use of warding off the bad with the good, in a similar list.
Says to repel with what is better, and describes what happens to an enemy afterwards.
Names the people this ayah is describing, and quotes what they said.

studies.applyIt: The next time somebody is short with you, try answering with something small and good rather than with silence or a matching remark. Not as a moral performance. Do it the way the ayah describes it, as a way of stopping the thing from continuing. Notice how often it works, and how rarely any of us try it.

studies.title: You Cannot Guide Whom You Love
studies.meaning: Two subjects sit in one passage. The first describes people of an earlier scripture who accepted the message: their mark is that they walk away from empty argument, leaving a farewell rather than a rebuttal, and decline the contest instead of winning it. The second turns to the Prophet and states a limit. Loving someone, even greatly, does not put their guidance in your hands. It is a statement about what a human being is able to do, not a reproach for having failed to do it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from late in the period before the emigration. The surah has been describing the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) among people who admired him personally and rejected what he brought. Classical sources connect the second ayah with his grief over a close relative who protected him for years without accepting the message, though the reports differ over details. What is clear is that the address shifts from describing believers to speaking to him directly.

keyTerms.note: Speech with nothing inside it: gossip, provocation, argument for its own sake. The root covers what is void and cancelled, so the word treats such talk as already worthless rather than as harmful.
To present one's side rather than one's face. The picture is of turning the body away from something without confronting it, a physical withdrawal from an exchange rather than a refusal shouted back.
A form implying the person has accepted guidance and taken it up, not merely received it. God is said to know these best, which places the assessment where no observer can reach.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public argument was a Meccan pastime. Men gathered near the sanctuary to trade verses and insults, and a crushing reply was remembered and repeated for years. Kinship set the rules of the contest: a man was answerable to his clan and defended by it, so a relative's position was never only a private opinion. To be loved by a kinsman who rejected your message was an ordinary and painful situation.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah's traditional name, The Stories, comes from a single word in ayah twenty-five, where Moses arrives in Madyan and recounts what has happened to him. The name marks the moment a fugitive tells his own history to a stranger, and it was taken from that scene rather than from the surah's larger sequence of narratives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is placed outside human control, including the control of a prophet. Two things follow. The impulse to force a conclusion loses its ground, because pressure cannot produce the thing being sought. And the believer is relieved of responsibility for another person's inner state while the duty to speak plainly remains, which separates faithfulness in speaking from success in persuading.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit in a different setting: their guidance is not upon you, and God guides whom He wills.
Asks directly whether the messenger would compel people, once it is granted that belief cannot be forced.
Names the grief this limit is addressed to, a messenger wearing himself out over those who refuse.

studies.applyIt: Think of the one person you keep trying to convince about something that matters to you. The next time you see them, say nothing about it at all, and ask instead about their week and listen to the answer. Notice how much of your attention was being spent on the argument, and where it goes when the argument is not running.

studies.title: Snatched From Our Land
studies.meaning: The objection is economic and it is stated plainly. If we follow the guidance with you, we will be torn out of our land. The reply does not argue with the fear; it points at what already exists. Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are gathered as provision from Us. Commentators note the shape of it. The security they are afraid of losing is offered as evidence about who has been supplying it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca's whole position rested on its sanctuary, which made the valley safe for pilgrimage and trade and drew goods from Yemen, Syria and the Gulf. No occasion of revelation is reported for the ayah with consensus, though commentators connect it generally to Meccans who found the message credible and feared what accepting it would cost their standing among the tribes.

keyTerms.note: Occurs once in the Quran. A verb for something grabbed suddenly, used of birds of prey, so the fear being described is of being seized rather than of being gradually squeezed out.
Occurs once in the Quran, from a root used for collecting revenue or water into one place. It describes goods converging on the valley rather than being produced anywhere inside it.
The word for what sustains, placed at the end of the list of fruits. It reclassifies a trading arrangement as a supply, which is the entire argument of the second half of the ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca grew nothing. The valley had no farmland, and the city ate what caravans brought, from Yemen in one direction and Syria in the other, and it could do that only because the sanctuary made the place safe to enter. Every Meccan understood that their food arrived because of an arrangement rather than because of any work done on the land.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran: the verb for being snatched away, and the verb for goods being gathered in. One names the fear and the other names what they already have. The rarest vocabulary in the sentence is spent on the two halves of a single anxiety about supply.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply treats a fear as evidence rather than as an obstacle. What the objectors do not want to lose is the very thing being pointed at as unearned, which turns the fear into an argument against itself. Nothing is promised in the ayah about their safety. What is offered is a reconsideration of where the safety they already have came from.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same point about the secure sanctuary, with people being seized all around it.
Names the same provision and security as the reason this city should serve its Lord.
Records the prayer that first asked for this place to be secure and provided for.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing you are most afraid of losing if you did the right thing: income, standing, a relationship. Then ask honestly where that thing came from in the first place. Not to talk yourself out of the fear. Only to see whether you have been treating something given to you as something you hold alone.

studies.title: Do Not Forget Your Share
studies.meaning: Four clauses, and the arrangement is where the sense lies. Two set direction: use what you have been given to seek the lasting home, and do not neglect the portion of this world that is yours. Two govern conduct: do good as good has been done to you, and do not work ruin in the land. Commentators differ over the portion mentioned. Some read it as what a person may rightly enjoy and use; others as the part of this life a person sends ahead, meaning their deeds. Both readings are early.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. These are the words of Qarun's own people to him. He belonged to Moses' community, had been given enormous treasure, and had turned it against them. The advice is quoted inside a surah addressed to a Meccan community with very little, facing opponents whose wealth was the main argument against the message. Placing the counsel in the mouths of ordinary people rather than a prophet is part of how the account works.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to set something upright and fixed, as a boundary stone is planted. The word implies an allotment already marked out, not a quantity a person negotiates upward.
From beauty as much as from benefit: doing a thing well and doing well by someone are one verb. The instruction is then measured against how God has acted, not against what others deserve.
The rotting of what was sound, used of meat, of water and of societies alike. It names damage done to something already working, which is why it attaches to those with the means to do it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that world was visible and it moved: herds, silver, worked cloth, and the number of people a man could feed. Generosity was competitive. Reputations were built by hosting travellers, paying compensation for men with no clan behind them, and freeing captives, and a rich man who kept everything was mocked in verse. Qarun's mistake would have been legible immediately to anyone hearing the account.
studies.didYouKnow: Qarun is named three times in the Quran. This surah tells his story at length, and the two other mentions place him alongside Pharaoh and Haman, in Surah 29 at ayah thirty-nine and Surah 40 at ayah twenty-four. The grouping is consistent: wealth, political power and administration named together as three forms of the same refusal.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The split between religious and worldly life is refused in a single sentence. What a person holds is treated as the material out of which the next world is sought, rather than as an obstacle to seeking it, and the enjoyment of one's own portion is protected in the same breath. The standard set for generosity is imitative: it is measured against what has been done for you, which removes calculation about who has earned it.

crossReferences.why: Keeps both worlds in one request, asking for good in this life and good in the next together.
Sends people out into the land to seek God's bounty as soon as the prayer has ended.
Gives the other half of the balance, this world as passing enjoyment set beside what lasts.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you own that you would be reluctant to lend: a tool, a car, a room, a book you care about. Lend it this week to someone who could use it, and pay attention to the specific reluctance rather than arguing with it. The passage does not ask you to hold nothing. It asks what the holding is for.

studies.title: Those Who Seek No Height
studies.meaning: The qualification is stated as two absences rather than an achievement: wanting no elevation on the earth and wanting no ruin on it. The order matters, and the commentators treat the second as what the first produces once it has room. Notice also that the word concerns rank desired, not rank held. A person can carry authority without wanting to be above anyone, and can want it fiercely while holding nothing. The final clause hands the outcome to the careful rather than to the strong.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah closes the account of Qarun, immediately after the ground opens on a man who had both wealth and the wish to be seen above his people. Most of those who had accepted the message in Mecca held no standing at all, and several were enslaved. The surah has been arguing that the visible arrangement is not the final one, and this is where it states the criterion plainly.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun from rising above. Because it names the wanting rather than the position, it can be present in someone with no power and absent in someone with a great deal.
From the heel, and so what follows behind. It is the word for how a thing ends up rather than how it looks now, which is why it can be assigned against present appearances.
From guarding oneself, originally the act of putting something between the body and a blow. It describes watchfulness rather than piety displayed, which suits a criterion about what a person wants.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Mecca was counted in visible things: how many camels a man watered, how many clients he protected, where he sat in the assembly, whether men rose when he entered. Precedence was tracked closely and disputed openly, and poets were paid to assert it. A society organised around that scoreboard would hear a criterion about not wanting height as the removal of the board itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with Pharaoh, described at its fourth ayah as having made himself high in the land, using the same root that appears here at the close. The surah therefore begins and ends on the same word: once as the description of a tyrant, and once as the thing the people of the final home do not want.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The criterion set here is interior and continuous rather than a list of acts, which places judgement on something no observer can audit. It also treats desire itself as accountable, so a person who never acquires power can still fail the test and a person who holds it can pass. The last clause moves the word for who wins in the end away from those who look like winning.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the same root, describing Pharaoh raising himself above the people of the land.
Connects arrogance on the earth with an inability to read signs, which explains the mechanism assumed here.
Puts the same disposition in terms of bearing, warning against the strutting and boastful walk.

studies.applyIt: Catch one moment today when you want to be known as the person who was right: a correction you could add to a thread, a fact you could supply that would settle who knew first. Let it go by without saying anything. Then notice how long the urge lasts, and whether anything at all was actually lost.
